'''''Phalaenopsis amabilis''''', commonly known as '''moon orchid''', '''moth orchid''',<ref name="CIA">{{cite web |title=ASEAN National Flowers |url=http://cia.sut.ac.th/ASEANInformation/AseanNationalFlowers.htm |publisher=Centre for International Affairs |accessdate=27 December 2018 |archive-date=14 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200814100714/http://cia.sut.ac.th/ASEANInformation/AseanNationalFlowers.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref> or '''mariposa orchid''',<ref name="Lo">{{cite news |last1=Lo |first1=Raymundo W. |title=What ails our orchid industry? |url=https://mb.com.ph/2023/03/07/what-ails-our-orchid-industry/ |access-date=13 March 2023 |work=Manila Bulletin |date=7 March 2023}}</ref> is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the orchid [[family (botany)|family]] Orchidaceae. It is widely cultivated as a decorative [[houseplant]]. It is an [[Epiphyte|epiphytic]] or [[Lithophyte|lithophytic]] [[Herbaceous plant|herb]] with long, thick roots, between two and eight thick, fleshy leaves with their bases hiding the stem and nearly flat, white, long-lasting flowers on a branching flowering stem with up to ten flowers on each branch.

''Phalaenopsis amabilis'' is native to [[Maritime Southeast Asia]], [[New Guinea]], and [[Australia]].<ref name="PoWO"/> It has three [[subspecies]]: ''P. a. amabilis'', native to the [[Philippines]] ([[Palawan]]), [[Malaysia]] ([[Borneo]]), [[Indonesia]] (Borneo, [[Sumatra]], and [[Java]]); ''P. a. moluccana'', native to the [[Maluku Islands]] ([[Seram Island|Seram]] and [[Buru Island|Buru]] Islands) and [[Sulawesi]] of Indonesia; and ''P. a. rosenstromii'', native to [[Papua New Guinea]] and Australia (northeastern [[Queensland]]).<ref name="Tsai">{{cite journal |last1=Tsai |first1=Chi-Chu |last2=Chou |first2=Chang-Hung |author2-link=Chou Chang-hung |last3=Wang |first3=Hao-Ven |last4=Ko |first4=Ya-Zhu |last5=Chiang |first5=Tzen-Yuh |last6=Chiang |first6=Yu-Chung |title=Biogeography of the Phalaenopsis amabilis species complex inferred from nuclear and plastid DNAs |journal=BMC Plant Biology |date=16 August 2015 |volume=15 |issue=1 |pages=202 |doi=10.1186/s12870-015-0560-z|pmid=26276316 |pmc=4537552 |doi-access=free }}</ref>

''Phalaenopsis amabilis'' is one of the three [[List of Indonesian floral emblems|national flowers of Indonesia]], where it is known as {{lang|id|italic=no|'''anggrek bulan'''}} (lit. "moon orchid").<ref name="CIA"/>

==Description==
''Phalaenopsis amabilis'' is an [[epiphytic]], rarely [[lithophytic]] herb with coarse, flattened, branching roots up to {{convert|1|m|ft|sigfig=2}} long and usually {{convert|3-4|mm|in|sigfig=2}} wide. Between two and eight fleshy, dark green, oblong to egg-shaped leaves {{convert|150-300|mm|in|sigfig=2}} long and {{convert|40-70|mm|in|sigfig=2}} wide are arranged in two rows along the stem. The stem is {{convert|100-300|mm|in|sigfig=2}} but hidden by the leaf bases. The flowers are arranged on a stiff, arching flowering stem {{convert|300-750|mm|in|sigfig=2}} long emerging from a leaf base, with a few branches near the tip. Each branch of the flowering stem bears between two and ten white, long-lasting flowers on a stalk (including the [[Ovary (botany)|ovary]]) {{convert|20-35|mm|in|sigfig=2}} long. Each flower is {{convert|60-70|mm|in|sigfig=2}} long and {{convert|50-80|mm|in|sigfig=2}} wide with the [[sepal]]s and [[petal]]s free from and spreading widely apart from each other. The sepals are egg-shaped, {{convert|30-40|mm|in|sigfig=2}} long and about {{convert|20|mm|in|sigfig=2}} wide and the petals broadly egg-shaped to almost square, {{convert|30-40|mm|in|sigfig=2}} long and wide. The [[Labellum (botany)|labellum]] is white with yellow and reddish markings, about {{convert|25|mm|in|sigfig=2}} long with three lobes. The side lobes curve upwards and partly surround the [[Column (botany)|column]]. The middle lobe is cross-shaped with a rounded tip and two long, thread-like wavy arms. There is a large yellow [[Labellum (botany)|callus]] near the base of the labellum. Flowering time depends on distribution but occurs from April to December in New Guinea.<ref name="Jones">{{cite book|last1=Jones|first1=David L.|title=A complete guide to native orchids of Australia including the island territories|date=2006|publisher=New Holland|location=Frenchs Forest, N.S.W.|isbn=1877069124|page=440}}</ref><ref name="ONG">{{cite web |title=''Phalaenopsis amabilis'' |url=http://www.orchidsnewguinea.com/orchid-information/species/speciescode/681 |publisher=Orchids of New Guinea |accessdate=26 December 2018}}</ref><ref name="POWO">{{cite web |title=''Phalaenopsis amabilis'' |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:650501-1 |publisher=Kew Science: Plant of the World Online |accessdate=26 December 2018}}</ref><ref name="ATROK">{{cite web |author1=D.L.Jones |author2=T.Hopley |author3=S.M.Duffy |author1-link=David L. Jones (botanist) |year=2010 |access-date=27 May 2021 |url=http://www.canbr.gov.au/cpbr/cd-keys/RFKOrchids/key/rfkorchids/Media/Html/Phalaenopsis_rosenstromii.htm |title=Factsheet - Phalaenopsis rosenstromii |website=[[Australian Tropical Rainforest Orchids]] |publisher=Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research (CANBR), [[Australian Government]]}}</ref>

==Taxonomy and naming==
In 1750, before the system of [[binomial nomenclature]] had been formalised by [[Carl Linnaeus]], [[Georg Eberhard Rumphius]] had collected the species on [[Ambon Island]] and described it as ''Angraecum albus majus'' in his book ''[[Georg Eberhard Rumphius#Herbarium Amboinense|Herbarium Amboinense]]''.<ref name="PoWO" /><ref name="Rumphius">{{cite book |last1=Rumphius |first1=Georg Eberhard |title=Herbarium amboinense (Volume 6)|date=1750 |location=Amsterdam |page=99 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/10356#page/144/mode/1up |accessdate=27 December 2018}}</ref> Linnaeus described it in ''[[Species Plantarum]]'' giving it the binomial ''Epidendrum amabile''<ref name="PoWO1" /><ref name="L.">{{cite book |last1=Linnaeus |first1=Carl |title=Species Plantarum (Volume 2) |date=1753 |location=Stockholm |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/13830#page/395/mode/1up |accessdate=26 December 2018}}</ref> and in 1825, [[Carl Ludwig Blume]] changed the name to ''Phalaenopsis amabilis''.<ref name="PoWO" /><ref name="Blume">{{cite book |last1=Blume |first1=Carl Ludwig |title=Bijdragen tot de flora van Nederlandsch Indië |date=1825 |location=Batavia |page=294 |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/9224#page/11/mode/1up |accessdate=26 December 2018}}</ref> The [[Botanical nomenclature|specific epithet]] (''amabilis'') is a [[Latin]] word meaning "lovely".<ref name="RWB">{{cite book|last1=Brown|first1=Roland Wilbur|authorlink1=Roland W. Brown|title=The Composition of Scientific Words|date=1956|publisher=Smithsonian Institution Press|location=Washington, D.C.|page =84}}</ref>

There are three subspecies of ''P. amabilis'' recognised by [[Plants of the World Online]]:
* ''Phalaenopsis amabilis'' subsp. ''amabilis''<ref name="PoWO1" /> which is the most widespread subspecies and is distinguished from the other subspecies by its cross-shaped labellum middle lobe, the base of which has yellow and red markings;<ref name="NCBI">{{cite journal |last1=Tsai |first1=Chi-Chu |last2=Chou |first2=Chang-Hung |last3=Wang |first3=Hao-Ven |last4=Ko |first4=Ya-Zhu |last5=Chiang |first5=Tzen-Yuh |last6=Chiang |first6=Yu-Chung |title=Biogeography of the ''Phalaenopsis amabilis'' species complex inferred from nuclear and plastid DNAs |journal=BMC Plant Biology |date=16 August 2015 |volume=15 |issue=1 |pages=202 |doi=10.1186/s12870-015-0560-z |pmid=26276316 |pmc=4537552 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
* ''Phalaenopsis amabilis'' subsp. ''moluccana'' <small>([[Schltr.]]) [[Eric Alston Christenson|Christenson]]</small><ref name="PoWO2" /> which has a linear-oblong labellum middle lobe, with a slight dilation at its base where there are yellow and white markings;<ref name="NCBI" />
* ''Phalaenopsis amabilis'' subsp. ''rosenstromii'' <small>([[F.M.Bailey]]) Christenson</small><ref name="PoWO3" /> which has a relatively short, triangular labellum middle lobe where the markings are yellow;<ref name="NCBI" />

In Australia, subspecies ''rosenstromii'' is recognised as ''Phalaenopsis rosenstromii'' by the [[Australian Plant Census]].<ref name="APC">{{cite web |title=''Phalaenopsis rosenstromii'' |url=https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/search?product=APC&tree.id=51209179&name=Phalaenopsis+rosenstromii&inc._scientific=&inc.scientific=on&inc._cultivar=&max=100&display=apc&search=true |publisher=Australian Plant Census |accessdate=27 December 2018}}</ref> It was discovered by Gus Rosenstrom "on trees, high from the ground, [[Daintree River]]" and was first formally described by [[Frederick Manson Bailey]] who published the description in the ''Queensland Agricultural Journal''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Phalaenopsis rosenstromii''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/473660|publisher=APNI|accessdate=27 December 2018}}</ref><ref name="AOF">{{cite web |title=''Phalaenopsis rosenstromii'', its systematics, distribution, conservation and propagation |url=https://www.australianorchidfoundation.org.au/302-2015/ |publisher=The Australian Orchid Foundation |accessdate=27 December 2018}}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Phalaenopsis amabilis'' usually grows on trees, rarely on rocks, in rainforest where the humidity is high but there is free air movement. Subspecies ''amabilis'' has the widest distribution and occurs from [[Palawan]] in the southern [[Philippines]] to [[Borneo]], [[Sumatra]] and [[Java]]. Subspecies ''moluccana'' is separated from subspecies ''amabilis'' by the [[Wallace Line]] and is found in [[Sulawesi]] as well as [[Seram]] and [[Buru]] in the [[Maluku Islands|Moluccas]]. Subspecies ''rosenstromii'' is native to New Guinea and [[Australia]] where it occurs on the [[Cape York Peninsula]] between the [[Iron Range, Queensland|Iron Range]] and the [[Paluma Range National Park]]. It is separated from subspecies ''moluccana'' by [[Richard Lydekker#Biogeography|Lydekker's Line]].<ref name="Jones" /><ref name="NCBI" />

==Conservation==
''Phalaenopsis rosenstromii'' was listed as "endangered" under the Australian Government [[Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act 1999]] but the listing was updated to ''Phalaenopsis amabilis'' subsp. ''rosenstromii'' in May 2016. The main threat to the subspecies in Australia is illegal collecting.<ref name="environment">{{cite web |title=Approved Conservation Advice for ''Phalaenopsis rosenstromii'' |url=http://www.environment.gov.au/biodiversity/threatened/species/pubs/87535-conservation-advice-05052016.pdf |publisher=Australian Government Department of the Environment |accessdate=27 December 2018}}</ref>

==Use in horticulture==
''Phalaenopsis amabilis'' is reported to be very easy to grow as a houseplant, as long as attention is paid to a correct feeding and watering regimen. It thrives in a domestic temperature range of {{convert|17-22|C|F|abbr=on}}, in bright indirect light such as that offered by an east- or west-facing window. Specialist orchid compost and feed is widely available. Species and cultivars in the genus ''Phalaenopsis'' are recommended for beginners.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.gardening-advice.net/phalaenopsis-orchid-care.html | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20100802105436/http://www.gardening-advice.net/phalaenopsis-orchid-care.html | url-status = usurped | archive-date = August 2, 2010 | title = Phalaenopsis Orchid Care Instructions | publisher = Organic Gardening Advice | accessdate = 24 April 2018}}</ref>

In cultivation in the [[United Kingdom]], ''Phalaenopsis amabilis'' has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/119644/i-Phalaenopsis-amabilis-i/Details
| title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Phalaenopsis amabilis'' | accessdate = 24 April 2018}}</ref><ref>{{cite web 
| url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 
| page = 76 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | accessdate = 24 April 2018}}</ref>

''Phalaenopsis amabilis'' is one of the parents of [[Phalaenopsis Harriettiae|''Phalaenopsis'' Harriettiae]], reportedly the first man-made ''Phalaenopsis'' hybrid, created by [[John Veitch (horticulturist)|John Veitch]] and recorded in 1887.<ref name=The_Garden_Dec11>{{cite journal |author=Sarah Forsyth |year=2011 |title=Top of the pots |journal=The Garden |volume=136 |issue=12 |page=33 |publisher=[[Royal Horticultural Society|RHS Media]] }}</ref>

==Importance==
''Phalaenopsis amabilis'' ({{langx|id|anggrek bulan}} meaning "moon orchid") is one of the three [[List of Indonesian floral emblems|national flowers]] in [[Indonesia]], the other two being the [[Jasminum sambac|sambac jasmine]] and [[Rafflesia arnoldii|padma raksasa]].<ref name="CIA" /> It was officially recognized as national "flower of charm" ({{langx|id|puspa pesona}}) in Presidential Decree No. 4 in 1993.<ref>[http://www.proxsis.com/perundangan/LH/doc/uu/F00-1993-00004.pdf Keputusan Presiden No. 4 Tahun 1993] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120402234237/http://www.proxsis.com/perundangan/LH/doc/uu/F00-1993-00004.pdf |date=2012-04-02 }}</ref>

The orchid is also the official flower of [[Kota Kinabalu]], the capital city of Sabah, Malaysia.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://dbkk.sabah.gov.my/index.php/ms/info-dbkk/info-korporat/maskot-bandaraya|title=Maskot Bandaraya}}</ref>
